You worked in New York before Miami. Which one is better for our clients?
Better for what? New York is bigger and the courts are faster. Miami is closer to the cargo.
And for you, personally?
Miami, easily. My morning is shorter, the office is smaller, and I speak Portuguese half the day.
So is the work less demanding here?
No, it is more demanding. The clauses are more complex, because everything crosses a border. In New York I had one jurisdiction. Here I have three.
Then which is the hardest part of the job?
The most difficult part is not the law. It is explaining to a client why the cheapest option is the slowest one. And your two programs — which one is more competitive?
This route is cheaper than the other one, but it is also slower.
Better for what? That changes the answer completely.

Eduardo, Nora here. I looked at your two programmes, and here are the numbers. London is older and more famous. Its admission rate is four per cent, the lowest in the country. The classes are bigger: sixty students. Miami is younger and less famous. Its admission rate is eighteen per cent, and the classes are smaller: twelve students. London is more expensive: thirty-one thousand a year, against nineteen. Miami is more convenient for you, because the campus is twenty minutes from your office.

Eduardo, Paulo Rezende. I compared the two ports for the March cargo, and the numbers are clear. Santos is bigger and busier. The freight is cheaper there: nineteen dollars a tonne, against twenty-two. But the queue is longer. The last vessel waited eleven days in Santos and three days in Paranagua. Eleven days cost us more than the freight. Paranagua is smaller, but it is faster, and the road from the farm is better in the rain. My decision is Paranagua.
